extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers learning algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and states foundational definitions, theorems, and criteria about varieties, separatedness, rational maps, proper/projective morphisms, abelian varieties, and Krull dimension used in algebraic geometry. Useful for understanding when objects/morphisms satisfy these properties and for applying the resulting consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety over a field k (Definition 11.3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: A variety over a field k, or k-variety, is a reduced, separated scheme of finite type over k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a reduced finite type affine k-scheme is a variety. This generalizes earlier notions of affine and projective varieties. Remarks: some sources additionally require irreducibility; some assume k algebraically closed. By Exercise 5.3.F the closed points of a variety are dense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subvariety
rubrics_metrics.description: A subvariety of a variety X is a reduced locally closed subscheme of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An open subvariety is an open subscheme (reducedness automatic); a closed subvariety is a reduced closed subscheme. One can quickly check a reduced locally closed subscheme is itself a variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of k-varieties (Proposition 11.3.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If k is perfect, the product (fibered product over Spec k) of k-varieties is a k-variety. (b) If k is algebraically closed, the product of irreducible k-varieties is irreducible. (c) If k is algebraically closed, the product of connected k-varieties is connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs reduce to the affine case and use separable closure or other exercises (e.g., Exercise 10.5.M). As an exercise one can avoid complications by alternative reductions (Exercise 10.4.H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of affine opens in a separated scheme is affine (Proposition 11.3.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a scheme and U and V are affine open subsets of X, then U ∩ V is affine (under the separatedness hypothesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses diagonal embedding and base change to an affine fibered product (Theorem 10.1.1). Warning: this property does not characterize separatedness (the correct property is 'affine diagonal'); counterexample: the line with doubled origin has the property but is not separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiprojective schemes are separated (Corollary 11.3.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every quasiprojective A-scheme is separated over A. In particular, every reduced quasiprojective k-scheme is a k-variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the structure morphism factors into open embedding, closed embedding, and P^n_Spec A (which is separated), and compositions of separated morphisms are separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universally injective morphisms (11.3.N–P)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is universally injective if it remains injective after any base change. Equivalent (exercise form): π is universally injective iff the diagonal morphism δ_π : X → X ×_Y X is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences/exercises: (a) universally injective morphisms form a reasonable class; (b) they are separated; (c) for finite type schemes over an algebraically closed field, universally injective ⇔ injective on closed points. Also stable under composition and base-change arguments (Exercises 10.4.G, 10.4.H, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus where two morphisms agree (Exercise 11.4.A and remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two morphisms π, π' : X → Y over Z, there exists a largest locally closed subscheme i : V ↪ X on which π and π' agree; V is closed if Y is separated over Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: V is given by a fibered product involving the diagonal δ : Y ↪ Y ×_Z Y and the map (π,π'): X → Y ×_Z Y. The locus can be nonreduced (example: maps π(x)=0 and π'(x)=x^2 on A^1 agree at x=0 but scheme-theoretically on Spec k[x]/(x^2)). Beware morphisms that agree as set-maps but differ as morphisms (e.g., Spec C → Spec C over Spec R: identity vs conjugation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced-to-Separated Theorem (Theorem 11.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two S-morphisms π, π' : U → Z from a reduced scheme U to a separated S-scheme Z that agree on a dense open subset of U are equal (π = π').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: the locus V where they agree is a closed subscheme containing a dense open; on a reduced scheme the only closed subscheme with dense underlying set is the whole scheme. Consequences: rational maps from reduced X to separated Y have a largest domain of definition; rational functions on reduced schemes have largest domain; indeterminacy locus notion; nonreduced source or nonseparated target gives counterexamples (Exercise 11.4.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphs of rational maps (11.4.4 & 11.4.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rational map π : X ⇢ Y (X reduced, Y separated), define the graph Γ_π as the scheme-theoretic closure of the graph of any representative morphism U → Y inside X × Y; this graph is independent of the representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The product should be taken in the category in which you're working (e.g., k-schemes). Use separatedness to view graphs of morphisms as closed embeddings; closure yields a well-defined graph for the rational map. Exercises show independence of representative and useful diagrams (cf. Figure 11.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of extension over an effective Cartier divisor (Exercise 11.4.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X is a Z-scheme and Y a separated Z-scheme, and D ⊂ X is an effective Cartier divisor. Any Z-morphism X  ackslash D → Y can be extended in at most one way to a Z-morphism X → Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: reduce to the affine case X = Spec A and D cut out by t ∈ A, then show the scheme-theoretic image arguments and inclusions A → A_t imply uniqueness. This is an application of separatedness and closure arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated-to-Separated Theorem (Exercise 11.4.H)
rubrics_metrics.description: If U is a locally Noetherian scheme and Z is separated over S, then two S-morphisms from U to Z that agree on an open subset containing the associated points of U are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extends the Reduced-to-Separated theorem to nonreduced locally Noetherian sources by focusing on associated points which control the scheme-theoretic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper morphism (Definition 11.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is proper if it is separated, of finite type, and universally closed (i.e., for every base change Z → Y, the base-changed map X ×_Y Z → Z is closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: in topology, a continuous map is proper if preimages of compact sets are compact. For schemes, universal closedness is the analogue; the 'universally' is crucial (A^1_C → Spec C is separated, finite type and closed but not proper because a base change can fail to be closed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of proper morphisms (Proposition 11.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Properness is stable under base change. (b) Properness is local on the target. (c) Properness is closed under composition. (d) Product of proper morphisms is proper. (e) If τ in a commutative diagram is proper and ρ is separated, then π is proper (cancellation-type statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These follow because separatedness, finite type, and universal closedness are 'reasonable' classes preserved by the indicated operations. Use these properties to build and recognize proper morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples: closed embeddings and finite morphisms are proper (Examples 11.5.2 & Proposition 11.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed embeddings are proper. Finite morphisms are proper (finite ⇒ affine + finite type, remain finite under base change, finite maps are closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closed embeddings are affine hence separated and finite type; closedness preserved by base change. For finite morphisms, finiteness is preserved by base change, and finite maps are closed (Exercise 8.3.L).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective schemes are proper (Theorem 11.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Projective A-schemes are proper over A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: The structure morphism factors as a closed embedding into P^n_Spec A followed by P^n_Spec A → Spec A. Closed embeddings are proper and composition of proper morphisms is proper; it suffices to show P^n_Spec A is universally closed, which reduces (by locality on the target) to the Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory (Theorem 8.4.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Global functions on connected reduced proper k-schemes (11.5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a connected reduced proper k-scheme with k algebraically closed, then Γ(X, O_X) = k (i.e., every global function is constant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: a global function gives a map X → A^1; extend to a proper map to P^1 and use connectedness to see the image must be a point. Scheme-theoretic image arguments then show the map is constant. Counterexamples appear if hypotheses are relaxed (e.g., k ≠ k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness characterization (11.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For locally Noetherian schemes: a morphism is finite iff it is proper and affine, equivalently proper and quasi-finite (Theorem referenced: 29.6.2 to be proved later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: a quasi-finite morphism from a proper scheme to a separated scheme is finite (use cancellation for proper morphisms to deduce properness of the map, then quasi-finite+proper ⇒ finite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abelian variety (Definition 11.5.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: An abelian variety over a field k is an algebraic group that is geometrically integral and projective over k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At this stage no concrete examples beyond elliptic curves are given; analytification over C gives a complex torus C^n / Λ. Remarks: algebraic groups are automatically quasi-projective; abelian varieties will later be shown to be commutative (abelian) using properness and the Rigidity Lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity Lemma (11.5.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be proper, Y geometrically integral with a rational point p, and let α : X × Y → Z be a morphism that is constant on X × {q} for some q ∈ Y (i.e., α|_{X × {q}} is constant). Then (a) there exists ψ : Y → Z with α = ψ ∘ pr_2 on X × Y (i.e., α factors through Y); (b) if α is also constant on {p} × Y then α is constant on all of X × Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses properness (to show images are closed and control fibers), geometric integrality (to get reducedness/irreducibility properties after base change), and reduction to dense open subsets. Exercises guide through fiberwise arguments and use that maps of varieties over algebraically closed fields are determined by closed points (Exercise 11.4.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms from abelian varieties factor as translation+homomorphism (Corollary 11.5.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is an abelian variety and G a group variety, any morphism φ : A → G is the composition of a translation and a homomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: compose φ with translation to send identity to identity, then build α(a1,a2) = φ(a1a2) φ(a1)^{-1} φ(a2)^{-1}. This α is constant on {e_A} × A and on A × {e_A}, so apply the Rigidity Lemma to deduce α is constant, forcing φ to be a homomorphism up to translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension of topological spaces and rings (Definition 12.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dimension of a topological space X (dim X) is the supremum of lengths of chains of closed irreducible subsets (indexing starts at 0). The dimension of a ring A is the supremum of lengths of chains of nested prime ideals (Krull dimension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convention: dim ∅ = −∞. Relationship: dim Spec A = dim A (use bijection between irreducible closed subsets of Spec A and prime ideals, Exercise 3.7.F). Examples: dim A^1_k = 1, dim Spec Z = 1, dim Spec k = 0. Nilpotents do not affect Krull dimension: dim Spec A = dim Spec A / N(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equidimensional / pure dimensional spaces (12.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological space is equidimensional (pure dimensional) if each of its irreducible components has the same dimension; equidimensional of dimension n means all components have dimension n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension is not a local property: if Z = X ∪ Y then dim Z = max(dim X, dim Y). Terminology: equidimensional dimension 1 is a curve, dimension 2 a surface, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension via affine covers (Exercise 12.1.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme has dimension n iff it admits an open cover by affine opens of dimension at most n, with equality achieved for some affine open subset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful equivalence: for any topological space X and open U ⊂ X, irreducible closed subsets of U correspond to irreducible closed subsets of X that meet U. Use this when reducing dimension statements to affine pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibers of integral morphisms have dimension 0 (Exercise 12.1.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is integral, then every nonempty fiber of π has dimension 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to Y = Spec k (a field) and show an integral finite type k-algebra has dimension 0: any nonzero element is integral over a field and thus invertible by looking at its minimal monic polynomial (nonzero constant term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension preserved under integral extensions (Exercise 12.1.F)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Spec B → Spec A corresponds to an integral extension of rings A → B, then dim Spec A = dim Spec B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Going-Up theorem to lift chains of primes downstairs to upstairs (same length), and show that two distinct primes upstairs cannot map to the same prime downstairs in a chain context (use Exercise 12.1.E to argue fiber dimensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjection of integral domains of same dimension implies isomorphism (Exercise 12.1.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: A surjection A → B between integral domains of the same dimension must be an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a simple dimension-counting exercise: if A → B is surjective and domains have same Krull dimension, kernel must be zero; combine with previously stated facts about primes and dimension.
